text.p: Lufthansa AG said on Thursday it would end the first half of 1997 with profits significantly higher than in the 1995 and 1996 periods due to strong passenger growth and cost-cutting at the German airline.
Lufthansa said the six-month performance prompted it to predict that it could top the record 1995 results for the full year, provided industry conditions did not change.
"In the absence of major changes in the market, we expect 1997 results to be above the best-ever results in 1995," Lufthansa Chairman Juergen Weber said at the airline's annual general meeting.
Lufthansa's final first-half results, to be released on August 26, would top results from the same periods in 1995 and 1996 and even exceeded the airline's expectations, Weber said.
"We will end the first half of this year with profits significantly higher than the prior-year level and also above the good half-year results in 1995," Weber said.
Lufthansa had hoped to post record earnings in 1996 when it reported a profit from ordinary activities of 686 million marks ($398 million) on sales of 20.8 billion marks.

But hopes for a record profit last year were dashed by higher fuel and operating costs, which Weber said rose eight percent to 22.2 billion marks. Weber noted that current oil prices were not expected to rise during the rest of 1997.

In addition to cost-cutting measures aimed at slashing 1.5 billion marks, or 20 percent, off Lufthansa's operating costs in the coming years, Weber said the airline's "Star Alliance" partnership contributed 200 million marks to 1996 profits.
Lufthansa offers code-share flights with airlines that include United Airlines, Thai Airways International, Air Canada and Scandanavian Airlines System.
"The barometer is presently rising. Our passenger numbers are growing strongly, especially in the North Atlantic, Asian and Pacific markets," Weber said.

Passenger traffic on South American routes has recently been up about nine percent, while North American traffic has been up 8.5 percent. But Weber said the German market has failed to show much improvement.

"Demand so far this year has been lively," he said of flights to North and South America. "It has never been so good." Weber also said results in Lufthansa's cargo business "are improving distinctly".

Shareholders at the meeting were also set to vote on measures tied to the Bonn government's plans to sell off its remaining 36 percent stake in the airline and efforts to ensure that a majority of Lufthansa remains in the hands of Germans.
The measures, which include giving Lufthansa the right to buy shares if the percentage of foreign ownership rises above 40 percent, were expected to be given shareholder approval.
Lufthansa, which has only one major German shareholder with a 10 percent stake, must remain in majority control by Germans to guarantee the country's bilateral flight agreements.

The German government, which transferred its shares to the Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau (KfW) for 2.1 billion marks in December 1996, intends to sell the Lufthansa shares in the autumn. No decision has been made on how the shares will be sold.
